deep.reconstruction:
Folio 140 (modern folio [106]) of the 1805 Brouillons, headed 'Zweite Hypothese' (second hypothesis), apparently with 'Litt. N.' in the header. The page is almost entirely columns of 7-digit logarithms and angles in sexagesimal notation. It is a numerical iteration in the orbit determination of a minor planet (very probably Pallas, given the previous page's 'Pall.'). The previous page carries out the first hypothesis; this page repeats the cycle with changed starting values and then does a further correction (a third pass, labelled with primes '''). I describe the structure and note where my reading is inferred.

(1) Left block, 'z'' = 2,550584'. A trial value of a distance-type quantity z'' (with the constant 0,588501 added on the first line) is used to find an angle: log 2.550584-type entries are combined with logs 0,4968031 + 9,9355774 = 0,4323805 and 0,0131560, giving 2,6255753 and, after subtracting 2147064 (= 0.2147064, the e'' of the previous page), 2,4108689. Then 4,8469619 and further log lines give 0,3866939 / 0,8186050 / 1,2052989 and 0,0111900. The sums 15,635396 + 2,550587 = 18,185983 show the closing of a linear relation (z'' + 15.635396 = 18.185983, i.e. e' = -18.185983 of the previous page used with opposite sign). The reproduced z'' = 2.550587 compared with the starting 2.550584 is the convergence check of the hypothesis. The adjacent column (7°31'5"75, 9.5271398, 0.4066397, 9.9962503, 0.4103894, 9.7191039, 1.2311682, 19.11.5,75) is a trigonometric reduction: an angle 7°31'5"75 is turned into 19°11'5"75 via log sin/cos style entries (9.9236804 appears repeatedly as a constant log). Below it, 13°14'17"04 = 8°12'15.72 + 5°2'1.32, and 3°10'14"40 = 8°12'15.72 - 5°2'1.32: that is half-sum and half-difference of two angles (a standard sum/difference device, as in Gauss's equations for eccentric anomaly differences).

(2) Below that, two three-fold column groups of log sines/cosines (9.1544373 / 9.9146600 / 9.9955323 etc., giving 66°53'46"62 and 55°4'21"53, and 7°19'24"19) are further spherical/plane-triangle reductions leading to 14°38'48"38 for the second angle. The three values 14°38'48"38, 12°18'38"48, 14°20'53"32 (with logs 0.4056985, 0.4069887, 0.4103894, 0.4155380) are three trial values of a quantity (probably an eccentric-anomaly-like angle or a logarithmic quantity) for neighbouring parameters, used for interpolation.

(3) Middle block: for each of the three trial values a small correction in seconds (1'16"59, 3'21"90, 5'5"66, and doubled 2'33"18, 6'43"80, 10'11"32) is added to give angles 3°4'39"62, 3°39'42"095, 3°35'13"39. These look like the mean anomaly interval M for the time interval between observations (the time-interval column in the previous page gave 3°40'36"7365 etc.), so this is solving the Kepler equation M = E - e sin E by trial: the following lines (6.87078.., 8.7298909, 3.74156.., 7.4597818 ...; 0.8333333.3; 0.8362332, +3; 0.4063436, 9.7014810; 0.7048626 ...) compute logs of sin E, e sin E in seconds (the constant 0.8333333.3 is the log of 206264.8..? Not exactly: 5.3144251 would be; instead 0.8333333 = 5/6, so it is probably a term proportional to 1/6 or 5/6 in a series expansion, unclear) and arrive at 0.0062062 / 0.0088386 / 0.0085664 and 65.0457 / 93.0858 / 90.1740, which are the residuals of the Kepler equation for the three trials. These are used for linear interpolation: log P''' = 0.0787904 and 0.0001888 (from 0.0801066 - 0.0013162 and 0.0003249 - 0.0001361), where P' and P'' of the previous page are corrected to P''' (the ratio of triangle areas or the correcting factor in Gauss's method of areas).

(4) Lower middle: e''' = 19.026031 - 0.838558 = 18.187473; log(1+P''') = 0.3422095, + 0.4764140 = log d''' = 0.8186235; and 0.3011244 + 9.6344448 = 9.9355692. These feed the next pass, the right-hand block, which starts again with z'' = 2.550333 (588501 added, 7°31'8"54, 19°11'11"16, 13°14'22"45, 3°10'17"19, 8°12'19"82, 5°2'2"63, 66°53'51"62, 55°4'21"29, 7°19'27"545, 14°38'55"09). The next page begins with 14°38'55"09 (0.4069560) and so the iteration is considered closed after this third pass (z'' changes from 2.550587 to 2.550333, i.e. 2.5e-4).

(5) Middle-bottom columns with 60683 21105 / 121248 75224 / 181981 and 96329 / 85652 / 9.6377762 log b' and 69706 17479 / 140534 87025 / 210240 / 104504 / 9.7089927 / 105736 / 9.7195663 log b'' are long-hand multiplications (partial products) for the logs of the coefficients b', b'' (the previous page had log b' 9.6376168, log b'' 9.7191039). Scattered figures in the lower margin (e.g. 4046661-42, 70-96, 31-38, 30-82) are scratch arithmetic.

What problem: this is the ordinary iterative solution of an elliptic-orbit determination for a small planet from three observations, with the hypothesis on the ratio of two geocentric distances corrected by successive passes until z'' agrees (Gauss's method of 1801-05, later in Theoria Motus Book II sec. 3). The surprising content is nil: the whole page is routine numerical labour, with the specific interpretation of individual columns uncertain from the image alone.
errors: The first-pass hypothesis z'' = 2.550584 and the recomputed value 2.550587 differ by 3 units in the last place, which is the normal convergence discrepancy rather than an error; the second trial agrees to about 2.5e-4 after the changed e'' (18.185983 -> 18.187473).

One cell in the lower-left block (the line after 0.0621121) was overwritten: the printed 9.6602458 is struck through and replaced by 9.6564176 (then written 9.656413? partly unclear); the struck-out value is the abandoned figure. Not an error in the final result.
I could not independently verify every logarithm line from the scan alone; the verification claims above are limited to sums that I could check.
The meaning of the constant 0.8333333.3 is uncertain from this page alone.

results.what: Iterative correction of an orbit-determination hypothesis (z'' and e'' passes) for a minor planet, with logs of P', P''', d''', b', b''
results.modern_name: Fixed-point iteration for the Gauss method of orbit determination from three observations (ratio-of-triangle-areas iteration)

results.what: Solution of the Kepler equation by trying three values of the eccentric anomaly and interpolating linearly on the residuals
results.modern_name: Kepler equation by trial-and-interpolation (regula falsi / secant)
results.usually_credited_to: Standard practice, 18th-19th century astronomers; Gauss's own Theoria Motus

results.what: Half-sum and half-difference of angle pairs (13°14'22"45 = 8°12'19"82 + 5°2'2"63; 3°10'17"19 = difference)

deep.surprise_reason: Purely numerical working for a minor-planet orbit (Pallas) using Gauss's well-documented logarithmic methods. Nothing here is a new result; the 'Zweite Hypothese' shows the iteration being repeated, which is exactly what is described in his published orbit-determination work.
